slides.title: The first conversation
slides.lead: Day 2 · Handling a Zillow Preferred lead with confidence
slides.body:
From the first hello
to a useful next step.

Learn the lead routes. Choose the right response. Guide the call with ALMS.
slides.notes: Teach the point and its reason, then read the example naturally. Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: Eric’s September 14 Day 2 objective.
slides.cue: Which part of the first call feels least comfortable today?

slides.title: What we’ll cover
slides.lead: Learn a piece, see an example, then try it.
slides.body:
1. Recognize and respond

    Read the three lead routes. Choose a call, text, or requested callback. Vote and write your response.

  2. Guide the conversation

    Introduce yourself, invite early, and use ALMS. Watch the examples, then practice discovery in pairs.

  3. Adapt and agree a plan

    Handle questions and changed circumstances. Watch a full call, then rotate agent, buyer, and observer in trios.

  4. Follow through

    Record what matters, keep your promises, and leave with a first-call reference.

Use your signed-in learner session for votes and short answers. Submit first; then we compare reasoning and reveal the example.
slides.notes: Teach the point and its reason, then read the example naturally. Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: September 14 objective.
slides.cue: Open your agent session now. We will pause for responses throughout.

slides.title: Three lead routes
slides.lead: Read the lead’s type and actual request before choosing your response.
slides.body:
Lead typeBuyer requestHow it reaches you
Connection / contact agentContact about a home for saleLive phone connection or FUB alert with contact preference
Real-time touringA tour, using availability supplied through ShowingTimeFUB alert; not a live call in TRU’s documented flow
Standard property tourA tour at a requested timeLive connection or FUB alert; requested time may still need availability checks

Example: “I requested 4 p.m.” on a standard tour is a requested time. “I’ll check access and confirm with you” keeps the request moving without promising unverified access.

slides.title: VOTE · Read the request
slides.lead: A standard tour lead asks for 5 p.m. The property’s availability is not confirmed. What do you do?
slides.body:
Compare with the teaching example

Acknowledge 5 p.m., check access, and tell the buyer when you will confirm. Their request gives you a starting point; it does not prove the seller approved it.

Use the requested time while keeping an unverified arrangement separate from a confirmed appointment.

slides.title: Choose the response that fits
slides.lead: Calls help you hear tone, ask follow-up questions, and build a relationship.
slides.body:
Already connected

Introduce yourself and help with the request. You are already on the call.

New alert, no preference

Call within five minutes of receipt during TRU’s 8 a.m.–8 p.m. operating window. If unanswered, follow with a personal text.

Text first / requested callback

Acknowledge by text now; honor the requested call time or explicit no-call preference.
slides.notes: Teach the point and its reason, then read the example naturally. Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: R008–R010; INT-009–INT-013, INT-054.
slides.cue: What would this change in your next buyer conversation?

slides.title: If the first call is unanswered
slides.lead: Make it easy for the buyer to recognize you and respond.
slides.body:
1. Call promptly

    Place the call within five minutes of receipt in the normal flow. Leave an opening voicemail when appropriate.

  2. Follow with a personal text

    Connect to the real inquiry and invite a phone conversation with genuine availability.

  3. Keep ownership

    Continue useful outreach while unanswered. The automated introduction is separate from your work.
slides.notes: Teach the point and its reason, then read the example naturally. Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: R009, R019.
slides.cue: What would this change in your next buyer conversation?

slides.title: “Text now” and “call at five”
slides.lead: Acknowledge the buyer now while respecting the plan they requested.
slides.body:
“Text is better right now.”

“Of course. I can help here. A quick call would also let us talk through the home and your plans—would this evening work?” Text now; do not record a permanent no-call preference.

“Call me at five.”

“Hi Maya, I’m Sam with Northside Realty, the agent who’ll call at five about your request. Let me know if you have questions before then.” Keep five unless the buyer agrees to change it.

“Please do not call me.”

Honor that request. Give useful help through the agreed channel.
slides.notes: Teach the point and its reason, then read the example naturally. Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: R008, R010; INT-013, INT-043.

slides.title: WRITE & DISCUSS · Choose your next message
slides.lead: Maya’s alert arrives at 2 p.m. and asks for a 5 p.m. call. Write your acknowledgment.
slides.body:
Compare with the teaching example

Hi Maya, I’m Sam with Northside Realty. I’ll be calling at five about your inquiry. If you have a question before then, let me know. I’m also free earlier if that would help.

Introduce yourself promptly, keep the requested call time, and offer earlier availability only if it is real. Do not call immediately just to satisfy the normal five-minute default.

slides.title: ALMS is your call framework
slides.lead: Start with a clear introduction. Then help with the appointment before discovery.
slides.body:
A

Appointment

Make it easy to meet.

L

Location

Understand where and what fits.

M

Motivation

Learn why it matters.

S

Summarize

Confirm what happens next.

Location and motivation can flow in either order. Listen to the person; do not recite a checklist.
slides.notes: Teach the point and its reason, then read the example naturally. Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: R012–R013; INT-015–INT-016.
slides.cue: What would this change in your next buyer conversation?

slides.title: Take the first turn
slides.lead: Orient the buyer: your name, brokerage, Zillow connection, and reason for the conversation.
slides.body:
Live connection

“Zillow connected us about your request…” fits a buyer already on the line. Begin warmly instead of waiting in silence.

Outbound call

“I’m calling about your request…” connects an unfamiliar number to something the buyer recognizes.

Use your real brokerage and role. Do not borrow claims about expertise or relationships that are not yours.
slides.notes: Teach the point and its reason, then read the example naturally. Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: R013; INT-016.

slides.title: VOTE · Now try the opening
slides.lead: Jordan asked to see 1234 Lane and has not requested a time. How would you begin?
slides.body:
Compare with the teaching example

Hi Jordan, I’m Sam with Northside Realty, a featured partner with Zillow. I’m calling about your request to see 1234 Lane. Would Saturday morning or afternoon work better? I’ll verify access for the time we choose.

Orient the buyer and offer useful times before discovery. Use actual availability. The invitation is a strong default, not a reason to ignore a buyer’s stated circumstances.

slides.title: Ask permission, then learn what fits
slides.lead: Explain why the questions will help the buyer.
slides.body:
Location

What attracted you to this area? What makes that location work for you?

Follow the answer

If they mention a shorter commute, ask what would improve. Do not jump to the next checklist item.
slides.notes: Teach the point and its reason, then read the example naturally. Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: R013; INT-016, INT-023.

slides.title: M · Motivation
slides.lead: Move from the feature to the reason behind it.
slides.body:
Buyer “We really want a bigger yard.”

Agent “What would you like to be able to do with that space?”

Buyer “I want room for a vegetable garden.”

Agent “That helps. What would the garden need from the space?”

“Big yard” is a feature. Gardening gives it meaning. Do not assume dogs, children, entertaining, or any other reason.
slides.notes: Teach the point and its reason, then read the example naturally. Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: R013; INT-016, INT-021.

slides.title: BREAKOUT · Ask the next question
slides.lead: Pairs: one buyer says “We need more space.” Ask permission, learn what that means, and follow their answer. Switch roles.
slides.body:
1 minute to set up · 2-minute conversation + 1-minute feedback/retry each way · 1-minute debrief. Switch buyer and agent after the first turn. Your presenter assigns groups; video rooms are in your meeting platform.

Compare with the teaching example

“What is feeling too tight in your current place?” Their answer could reveal the purpose of the space. Follow that answer rather than assuming a larger bedroom count solves it.

Choose a question connected to the buyer’s words. There is no required question count, personal anecdote, or fixed order for location and motivation.

slides.title: WRITE & DISCUSS · Close this call
slides.lead: Jordan wants garden space, prefers Saturday morning, and is open to another home. Access is still unconfirmed.
slides.body:
Compare with the teaching example

“The garden space is important, and Saturday morning is your preference. I’ll check access and find another useful comparison. I’ll send the confirmed details after I hear back. Is there anything I missed?”

Do not upgrade a requested time into a confirmed showing. Reflect the actual priorities and your promised action.

slides.title: “I just have questions.”
slides.lead: Help with the question; earn another invitation through useful service.
slides.body:
1. Acknowledge and capture

    “Of course—what would you like to know?” Answer accurately; say what you need to check.

  2. Learn the context

    With permission, understand what drew them to the home and how the answer affects their search.

  3. Offer a useful next step

    Explain how seeing the home could help. If they still decline, stop pushing and agree how you’ll bring back the answers.

Answers are not a reward for agreeing to a showing. Never guess or hide a known answer.
slides.notes: Teach the point and its reason, then read the example naturally. Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: R014; INT-016.
slides.cue: What would this change in your next buyer conversation?

slides.title: Keep the first meeting easy
slides.lead: Do not open with a demand for preapproval, budget, or proof they are ready to buy.
slides.body:
Why timing matters

They asked to see a home. A private financial interview from someone they do not know can turn that request into a barrier.

If the buyer asks

Answer their question. Learn enough context to make guidance useful; involve a lender for financing specifics.

The usual later opening

The end of the first showing offers context for a relevant financing conversation. A long buying timeline does not automatically rule out planning help.
slides.notes: Teach the point and its reason, then read the example naturally. Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: R001–R004; INT-001–INT-005, INT-016.
slides.cue: What would this change in your next buyer conversation?

slides.title: VOTE · Respond to their question
slides.lead: The buyer asks, “Should I talk to a lender before we look?” What is the best response?
slides.body:
Compare with the teaching example

“Happy to help. What timing do you have in mind for a move?” Use the context to explain a useful next step and offer lender help where it fits.

Buyer-initiated financing questions deserve an answer. Avoid both a blanket refusal to discuss money and a blanket requirement to obtain preapproval before receiving help.

slides.title: Answer honestly and keep helping
slides.lead: Answer the role question clearly, then return to how you can help.
slides.body:
Your role

“I’m not the listing agent. I help buyers and can coordinate with the listing side. What would you like to know?”

Availability

If the home is under contract, say so. Check any uncertain access; do not promise a showing.

Useful next step

Ask what attracted them to the home and offer relevant options, with their permission.

slides.title: WRITE & DISCUSS · Keep helping with the inquiry
slides.lead: On the first call, Jordan asks about a home that is under contract. You learn garden space matters. What do you say?
slides.body:
Compare with the teaching example

“The home is under contract. I can check whether a viewing is still possible. Since garden space matters, I can also research some options to compare. Would that be useful?” Keep access and unresearched alternatives conditional.

Tell the truth, use known priorities, keep possibilities conditional, and offer a next step. Do not merely hand the search back with “Want something else?”

Motivation “What else caught your eye?”

slides.lead: Trios: agent, buyer, observer. Run the full first call using the buyer card, give one specific correction, retry, then rotate until everyone has spoken.

1 minute to set up · three 4-minute rounds: 3-minute call + 1-minute correction/retry · 2-minute debrief. Rotate agent → observer → buyer so everyone speaks. Submit your reflection after your turn.

Compare with the teaching example

Introduce yourself, offer the appointment early, ask permission, explore location and motivation through follow-up questions, and summarize the actual plan. Adapt if Jordan has limited time or a different request.

Use a partner as the buyer. When studying alone, say the agent’s turns aloud and compare with the two demonstration slides. A self-check is practice, not observed coach sign-off.

slides.title: Follow through on what you promised
slides.lead: The next contact should have a reason the buyer recognizes.
slides.body:
After a conversation

Record their priorities, contact preference, pending access checks, and the exact next action you promised.

If unanswered

Day one: aim for three to four personal touches, at least two calls and one text. First week: ten total including day one, mostly calls.

Once they reply

Follow the conversation and agreed plan. Stop applying the unanswered-lead quota.

Set a task for the promised action. Use the buyer’s agreed channel and timing; a reply ends the unanswered-lead quota, not your responsibility to follow through.

slides.lead: Introduction → Appointment → Location / Motivation → Summarize

Before contact

Lead type · actual request · property · tour or callback time · contact preference

During the call

Orient them · offer the meeting · ask permission · follow an answer · propose useful comparisons

Before you finish

Restate priorities · distinguish confirmed from pending · explain the next step · record and follow through

cases.quote: I’d like to see 1234 Lane Saturday morning. The yard caught my eye.
